C08-M02-L05-F1.title: Same field name, different meaning across sources
C08-M02-L05-F1.caption: A field dictionary for four Banyan identifiers shows that src_ip, user, host and outcome mean different things in the VPN, proxy and Windows 4720 events.
C08-M02-L05-F1.alt: Table with four columns: Field, VPN log, Proxy log and Windows 4720. Row src_ip: VPN external client address; proxy internal workstation address; Windows 4720 not recorded. Row user: VPN account signing in; proxy user browsing; Windows 4720 subject, who created the account, with the new account in target_user. Row host: VPN no host field; proxy client workstation; Windows the machine that logged the event. Row outcome: VPN success or failure; proxy none, HTTP status instead; Windows success or failure.
C08-M02-L05-F1.note: New account in 4720 is in target_user; confirm each field's meaning per source before pivoting.

C08-M02-L05-F2.title: Normalisation: two raw formats, one ECS-style vocabulary
C08-M02-L05-F2.caption: normalise_demo.py parses a firewall syslog line and a VPN JSON record into the same field names, so one search on source.ip finds both.
C08-M02-L05-F2.alt: Graph flowing left to right. Firewall syslog (fw01), with SRC= and DPT=3389 and local IST time with no year, feeds the parser from_syslog(), which uses a regular expression and converts IST to UTC. VPN gateway JSON, with clientIP, user and result, feeds the parser from_vpn_json(), which decodes JSON and renames fields. The edge from from_syslog() is labelled SRC to source.ip and the edge from from_vpn_json() is labelled clientIP to source.ip; both arrive at ECS-style event, with @timestamp (UTC), source.ip, event.module and event.action. That node feeds One search: source.ip = 203.0.113.66, via an edge labelled matches both events.
